# What's the Future of Software Engineering?

Some questions I've found myself asking after changing the way I build software.

---

## 01 — Has the way we build software fundamentally changed, or am I taking the easier route?

Back in poly, building a website meant going through wireframes, looking for design inspiration and working through the implementation myself. This time, my approach was rather different. I used English to communicate my ideas to AI, explored templates through Stitch, referenced existing portfolios on GitHub and iteratively refined the design. I barely had to dive into the technical details of HTML or CSS.

My background in HTML certainly made the process easier, but I believe someone with little to no knowledge of it could have achieved something similar. Has the way we build software fundamentally changed, or am I simply taking the easier route? Is this the direction software development is heading, or am I overlooking something important by skipping the traditional process?

---

## 02 — What does it actually mean to know how to do something?

I understand the basics of Git, but when I encountered a merge conflict, I turned to AI for help. It suggested solutions, I implemented them and verified the results. I had an issue, a starting point and a desired end state. I managed to reach that end state successfully.

But does that mean I know how to resolve a merge conflict? Does that make me competent in Git? Must I understand every step and underlying mechanism to claim that I know how to do something, or is being able to identify a problem, find a solution and verify the outcome sufficient?

---

## 03 — Is working with a black box an acceptable trade-off?

One aspect I find particularly uncomfortable is treating AI-generated code as a black box.

One of the common criticisms of AI-assisted development is that it creates technical debt. Developers can produce working software without understanding how it actually works, leaving behind code that becomes difficult to maintain, debug or extend. To some extent, I find myself doing exactly that.

Coming from a pre-LLM software development background, it feels strange to simply trust an implementation I barely understand. Abstraction has always been part of software engineering, but there is a difference between relying on a well-established framework maintained by a community and relying on AI-generated code whose quality can be questionable. In a team, there may be other developers who understand and can take responsibility for different parts of the system. When building something independently with AI, who is accountable for the parts neither of us fully understands?

At the same time, I do have some fundamental knowledge. If something breaks, I can open the code, investigate the issue and work towards fixing it, even if I didn't write the original implementation. I can also use AI to generate more test cases and explore scenarios I might not have considered myself. This allows me to test features more extensively, despite not understanding every detail of the underlying code.

But is that enough? Does having the ability to investigate and troubleshoot when things go wrong make the technical debt manageable? Can more extensive testing compensate for a lack of understanding, or am I simply shifting the risk from writing the code to maintaining it?

---

## 04 — Where does my contribution end and AI's begin?

Perhaps this question extends beyond software engineering itself. Even this article raises a similar dilemma. I started by dumping my thoughts and questions onto the page. AI helped organise them, refine the wording and turn them into a coherent piece. The ideas are mine, but much of the writing is not.

So, is this article written by me, by AI, or some combination of both? At what point does using AI as a tool become having AI do the work for you?

---

## Where I stand

I don't have definitive answers to these questions. Am I worried about the future of software engineering? Yes, to some extent. But I am not particularly pessimistic. I remain confident in my ability to adapt, pick up new skills and solve problems.

What I am less certain about is how we should measure competence in a world where knowing how to do something and knowing how to get something done are increasingly different things.
